nb_main_wall_center_face.blurb: The tallest stretch of the long cliff band at Red Rock Mountain, a remote backcountry crag in southwestern New Brunswick. This is the largest wall there, with 28 routes that are almost all bolted sport lines and just a couple of trad lines. Grades run from easy 5.3 up past 5.11, but the bulk sit in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it suits solid leaders more than first-timers. The longest lines reach roughly 35 metres. The cliff gets plenty of sun and offers little shade, which makes spring and fall the comfortable seasons. Expect a quiet, wild feel, with poor phone coverage and no buildings nearby.

nb_cedar_point.blurb: A small abandoned limestone quarry tucked into a residential neighbourhood of Saint John, looking out toward the Bay of Fundy. Of its 25 climbs, most are bolted sport routes, with a handful of trad lines and one boulder problem. Grades start around 5.4 and stretch to the low 5.12s, with the greatest concentration between 5.7 and 5.11. The stone is solid and the faces include slabby sections that reward balance and footwork. Sun helps the rock dry quickly, though wind can funnel into the quarry and make it cold even in summer, so the shoulder seasons are often best. A good option for a short session close to town.

nb_pyramid_wall_area.blurb: One of the sections along the string of cliffs at Cochrane Lane near Welsford, north of Saint John. The wall is named for an enormous pyramid-shaped block set in its middle. Of the 24 climbs, nearly all are traditional lines, with one bolted route. Difficulty spans about 5.5 to the low 5.11s, with a good spread of moderates from 5.6 through 5.10, which makes it a friendly place for climbers building up their trad skills. The wider cliff is generally quiet, and midweek visitors often have it to themselves. Follow the trail markers and maps along the base of the cliffs to reach it.

nb_cape_spencer.blurb: A coastal bouldering spot at the end of the road past Saint John, on the Bay of Fundy shoreline near the lighthouse. Boulders and small cliffs sit along the shore, with 22 problems listed, from very easy up to about V3. Most are in the V0 to V2 range, so it works well for newer boulderers and warm-up sessions. The rock is hard, fine-grained and feature-rich, though it gets slick in the tidal zone and turns crumbly toward the outer ends. Landings are uneven, so bring a few pads. Tide timing shapes which blocks are usable, and it is a nice spot to watch seabirds and sea mammals between problems.

nb_the_hex_wall.blurb: A wall about 70 feet tall at Eagle Rock, one of the older climbing areas near Welsford, a short drive from Saint John. All 21 routes are traditional, and cracks dominate, from fist-sized to thin fingers, with a few steeper overhanging lines. Difficulty runs from very easy to the 5.12 range, though most routes fall in the 5.8 to 5.10 bracket. It is a good place to practise crack technique and gear placement. A short flagged trail leads in from the road. Watch for loose rock and small drops near the top of the cliff if you walk off.
nb_the_hex_wall.approach: From the road, continue roughly 150 m beyond the small cairn and find the pink flagging tape, then follow the trail up through the trees to the wall.

nb_pooh_corner.blurb: A compact corner of the large Cochrane Lane cliffs near Welsford, set between the Cheekbone and Waterfall Wall sections. Of the 21 climbs, 20 are trad and a single winter ice line gives it a cold-season option too. Some routes are multi-pitch, which is unusual on this cliff. Grades begin at 5.8 and are spread evenly through the 5.9, 5.10 and 5.11 ranges, with a few climbs in the 5.12s and beyond, so it leans toward experienced climbers. The trail in passes the Gollum area, then heads toward Cheekbone Corner before cutting up and left.
nb_pooh_corner.approach: Take the side trail past the Gollum area, climb toward Cheekbone Corner, then continue up and left to the base.
